Do squatters have rights in Delaware?

In Delaware, a person with no permission can claim title to land only by adverse possession, and the possession has to last twenty years. A short stay in someone's vacant house does not create ownership, and an owner who acts early has strong options.

The Delaware Code does not use the words "squatter" or "adverse possession" in the real actions chapter. It works through time limits. Title 10, chapter 79 says a person may not enter land unless within 20 years after the person's right or title first accrued, and may not sue on a prior possession unless there was actual possession within 20 years before the action. Delaware courts have built the adverse possession elements on that twenty-year rule.

Two kinds of situations get lumped under "squatters," and the law treats them differently:

  • Long-term occupants with a claim to own: neighbors who have used a strip or a whole parcel for decades, or co-owners and heirs who stayed in an inherited house.
  • Short-term unauthorized occupants: people who moved into a vacant home or stayed after a lease or permission ended.

What must a person prove to win adverse possession in Delaware?

The claimant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, possession that is open and notorious, hostile and adverse, exclusive, and actual, and continuous for twenty years. That is how a Master in Chancery summarized the test in the 2020 report in Estate of Waples v. Burton.

  • Open and notorious: public enough that the owner and others have notice. The report says furtive possession is not adverse.
  • Hostile: use that is inconsistent with the owner's rights. The claimant does not have to announce an intent to own, but must act as the owner, to the exclusion of others.
  • Exclusive and actual: the report says absolute exclusivity is not required and that fences and signs are not required in every case.
  • Continuous for twenty years: the report treats the period as a bright-line inquiry, and successive possessors can add their time together (tacking) if they are in privity.

Once the claimant meets the burden, the record owner must show by a preponderance that the use was permissive. The Delaware Supreme Court's 2004 order in Dorman v. Mitchell restated the test as possession in an "open, notorious, hostile and exclusive manner for a twenty-year period" and held the claimant's title vested in 1991, years before the new owners learned of the property.

Permission defeats the claim. Where a landlord-tenant relationship exists, the use is permissive. In Waples, a missing rent payment for about 37 years was held to extinguish a tenancy, which shows that facts, not labels, decide these cases.

Can an heir or co-owner claim an inherited Delaware house by adverse possession?

It is harder for a co-owner. The Waples report says that when one co-tenant claims the whole property, the claimant must show ouster of the others, proved with more than would be needed against a stranger.

Ouster requires three things: intent, adverse possession in fact, and the other co-tenants' knowledge or notice of the adverse claim. The Master found that paying taxes and sewer charges, which began as a voluntary contribution, did not by itself show ouster. The claimant never clearly told the other co-tenants that she excluded them or claimed sole ownership, and the other co-tenants' use was substantial. The report recommended summary judgment for the co-tenants.

For families, this has a practical side. One heir living in and paying for an inherited house does not automatically become the owner by staying for twenty years. If heirs disagree about who owns a house, a sale can settle the question. Consult a Delaware attorney about who has authority to sell.

Does the 10-year disability extension apply?

Sometimes. Under 10 Del. C. section 7903, a person who is an infant, mentally ill or imprisoned when the right accrues may enter or sue within 10 years after the disability ends, even if the 20-year period has run. Section 7904 gives successors in title the same benefit if the person dies while under the disability.

For an owner this matters at the edges. If title was held by a minor heir, the clock may not have run against that heir. A title company will want to know about such facts before insuring a sale.

How do Delaware owners remove an occupant with no right to be there?

An owner should use the courts, not self-help. Delaware's summary possession statute, 25 Del. C. chapter 57, lets a landlord or owner file a complaint in the Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property sits. Section 5703 allows the landlord, the owner or a wrongfully excluded tenant to file.

The statute lists grounds that include holdover after a lease ends, unpaid rent and lease violations. A complaint is filed with the court, which serves it with a hearing notice. The notice and complaint must be served 5 to 30 days before the hearing, and the court's rules provide for service by posting and mailing when personal service fails.

After judgment, a writ of possession issues once the appeal period passes, with at least 24 hours' notice, and execution happens between sunrise and sunset. A party can seek a new trial or review within 5 days under section 5717. Cases may be sent to mediation under the eviction diversion program in section 5702A.

The Justice of the Peace Court instructions say a complaint for summary possession needs the rental unit address, a short statement of facts, the relief sought and the filing fee. Those instructions do not address non-tenants, so an owner whose occupant never had a lease should speak with a Delaware attorney about the right filing.

What is the risk of locking someone out in Delaware?

If the person is a tenant, a lockout can cost the owner treble damages. Under 25 Del. C. section 5313, a tenant removed or shut out by the landlord or the landlord's agent can recover possession or end the rental agreement, and can recover three times the rent per diem for the period of exclusion, or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus court costs. The statute does not apply when the removal happens under color of a valid court order.

An occupant's status is the key fact. Someone who was a tenant even briefly may have tenant protections. Documentation of the lease, rent receipts and messages helps the court see the facts.

Criminal trespass is also in the Delaware Code. Third degree, section 821, covers knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully on real property and is a violation. Second degree, section 822, covers a building or an enclosed property manifestly designed to exclude intruders and is an unclassified misdemeanor.

How can an owner protect a vacant Delaware house from a claim?

Regular visits and written records are the best protection against a stranger's claim. Adverse possession needs open and notorious use over twenty years, so an owner who checks the house and reacts promptly undermines the claim long before the period runs.

  • Inspect vacant or inherited property on a schedule and keep dated notes and photos.
  • Secure doors and windows and post the owner's contact information.
  • Give written permission to any neighbor who uses a strip of the land, since permission defeats the hostile element.
  • Pay taxes and keep records of who is in the house.
  • Act quickly through the courts if an unauthorized occupant appears.

A vacant house with a possible occupant, back taxes or unclear heirs can be hard to sell on the open market. Cash Home Buyers buys houses as-is in many situations, but a title search will show whether a claim has to be resolved first.

Frequently asked questions

How long does adverse possession take in Delaware?

Twenty years. Delaware courts require possession that is open and notorious, hostile, exclusive, actual and continuous for the full twenty-year period, and the claimant must prove each element by a preponderance of the evidence.

Can paying property taxes give someone title in Delaware?

Not by itself. In the Waples report, a co-tenant's payment of taxes and sewer charges did not prove ouster of the other owners. The claimant still had to show every element of adverse possession.

Does permission stop adverse possession?

Yes. Use with the owner's permission is not hostile. A Chancery report says that once the claimant meets the burden, the record owner must show the use was permissive.

Can I change the locks on a person living in my Delaware house?

Not safely without a court order if the person is a tenant. Section 5313 allows a locked-out tenant to recover treble damages or three times the per diem rent, whichever is greater. Talk to a Delaware attorney first.

Which Delaware court handles removal of an occupant?

The Justice of the Peace Court for the county where the property is located hears summary possession cases under 25 Del. C. chapter 57. Adverse possession ownership claims have been decided in the Court of Chancery and reviewed by the Delaware Supreme Court.

Can I sell a house that has an occupant I want removed?

Often yes, but a title company will check for any claim of right. A buyer who purchases as-is may take on the removal, so disclose the occupant early.

Can a Delaware landlord end a tenancy just because the house is being sold?

Not on that ground alone, as far as the code we reviewed shows. The grounds for summary possession in 25 Del. C. 5702 do not list a sale of the property, so an owner who wants a vacant house has to use the notice rules that apply to the tenancy.

Under 25 Del. C. 5106, a landlord may end a fixed-term agreement by giving at least 60 days' written notice before the term expires, stating that it ends on its expiration date. A month-to-month tenancy needs 60 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the month after actual notice. An agreement that is not in writing cannot be effective for longer than one year, and one with no stated term is treated as month-to-month.

If a lease runs a year or more and neither side gives notice at least 60 days before it ends (45 days for the tenant), section 5108 turns it into a month-to-month tenancy on the same terms. A seller who misses that window can end up with a tenant in place at closing.

How can a seller show a rental to buyers?

A landlord must give 48 hours' notice before entering and may enter only between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. That comes from 25 Del. C. 5509, and it covers showings as well as repairs.

  • The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to exhibit the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants.
  • The 48-hour notice can be waived in a signed addendum or separate signed document for prospective tenants or purchasers only.
  • Emergencies allow entry at any time.
  • A landlord cannot use access to harass a tenant, and repeated unreasonable entry can be treated by the tenant as grounds to terminate.
  • Section 5510 makes the landlord liable for theft, casualty or other harm from entry made without the tenant's consent when the tenant is absent or present and able to consent.

Photos, lockbox visits and open houses all need to fit those limits.

What happens to a tenant's retaliation protection during a sale?

Retaliation rules still apply, but a good-faith sale can be a defense. Section 5516 bars a landlord from seeking possession, raising rent or cutting services after a tenant makes a good-faith code complaint, organizes other tenants or pursues a legal remedy, and it presumes retaliation when the landlord acts within 90 days.

Paragraph (d)(7) gives a defense where the landlord has in good faith contracted to sell and the contract of sale contains a purchaser representation that the buyer will use the unit as the buyer's own residence, substantially alter or demolish it, or stop renting it for at least six months. A tenant who proves a violation can recover three months' rent or treble damages, whichever is greater, plus costs but excluding attorneys' fees.

Practical point: if a tenant made a repair complaint a few weeks ago, timing a notice around the sale invites a retaliation claim. Fix the complaint first, then plan the exit.

What notice must a landlord give for unpaid rent or a lease violation?

Seven days is the minimum in both cases. These are the steps in Chapter 55 and Chapter 57 of Title 25.

SituationNotice or stepSection
Unpaid rentWritten demand giving not less than 7 days before the landlord may file to terminate5502
Material lease breachWritten notice with at least 7 days to cure5513
Rent paid in full before filingLandlord may not file for possession on that ground5502(c)
Holdover after the term endsTenant owes up to double the monthly rent, prorated daily5515
Late feeCapped at 5 percent of monthly rent and not imposed within 5 days of the due date5501(d)

Section 5513 lets a landlord rely on the notice for a substantially similar breach within one year. Where a breach causes or threatens irreparable harm, the landlord may terminate on notice without the cure period.

How does an eviction case work in Delaware?

Possession cases go to the Justice of the Peace Court. Section 5701 puts an action for summary possession in the Justice of the Peace Court that hears civil cases in the county where the rental is located.

  • The landlord files a complaint for possession, and the court serves the complaint with a notice of the hearing time and place (section 5704).
  • Under section 5702A, after filing, the case is scheduled for mediation through the court's residential eviction diversion program. Mediation must be completed at least 48 hours before trial, and a tenant's failure to engage does not delay trial.
  • Section 5704A requires lead-based paint documentation with the complaint.
  • Notices must be served personally, left with an adult at the unit, or mailed, and posting works only when combined with a return receipt or certificate of mailing (section 5113).

The other grounds in section 5702 include holding over after the agreement ends, deducting wrongfully from rent, breaching a lawful obligation, holding over more than 5 days after a foreclosure sale with perfected title, and a sole tenant's death. Section 5115 allows an expedited forthwith summons where a tenant has caused substantial or irreparable harm.

Self-help is not an option. The Delaware code abolishes the landlord's right of distress for rent in section 5120, and a lease clause for attorneys' fees is unenforceable under section 5111.

What should a seller do about a tenant's belongings and keys?

If a landlord wins possession and there is no appeal, the landlord may remove and store the tenant's items at the tenant's expense. Seven days after the appeal period expires, the property is deemed abandoned and may be disposed of without further notice or liability (section 5507(e)).

Section 5125 covers keys. A lease cannot require surrender before the end of the term, and where there is more than one tenant possession is returned only when all of them have complied. Document everything with photos, dates and written notices.

On the money side, a landlord who sells should know that a tenant's surety bond travels with the lease. Under section 5514A(j), if the landlord's interest is sold or transferred, the new landlord must accept the tenant's surety bond and may not demand an additional security deposit during the current term.

What does the Delaware rental market look like for owners?

Delaware has about 402,000 households and a statewide median gross rent of $1,401. Rentals are a minority, since about 73% of occupied homes are owner-occupied.

Several sections, including 5102 and 5512, have versions that take effect March 8, 2027, and the source-of-income fair housing rules in section 5116 have a different version effective December 31, 2028. Check the current text before you act.

When a rental becomes a burden, a cash buyer can purchase the house with the tenant in place or after the tenant leaves, on terms you negotiate. We are not attorneys, so have counsel review notices and the lease first.

Frequently asked questions

How much notice must a Delaware landlord give to end a month-to-month tenancy?

At least 60 days in writing, counted from the first day of the month after actual notice, under 25 Del. C. 5106(d). The tenant gives the same notice to end it.

How much notice does a landlord need to enter to show a rental?

At least 48 hours, and entry is allowed only between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. under 25 Del. C. 5509. Emergencies are the exception, and a tenant can sign a waiver of the 48 hours for prospective purchasers.

Where are Delaware eviction cases filed?

In the Justice of the Peace Court that hears civil cases for the county where the rental sits. After filing, the case is scheduled for mediation before trial.

Can a tenant stay if the landlord sells the house?

The sale is not listed as a ground for summary possession, so the landlord still has to end the tenancy through the lease terms and the notice rules. A buyer should ask for the lease and any notices before closing.

What if a tenant stays after the lease ends?

The tenant owes up to double the monthly rent, prorated daily, for each day of holdover under section 5515. The landlord must still use the court process to regain possession.
